title: Red Sox shortstop Marcelo Mayer lands on IL with bone stress reaction in forearm
content:
BOSTON — The infield depth for the Boston Red Sox took yet another hit Friday as shortstop Marcelo Mayer landed on the injured list with a bone stress reaction in his left forearm.

Mayer said he’s been dealing with the forearm pain on and off for the last two months.

“Some days have been worse than others,” he said. “But just had a talk with the medical staff, with the doctors, and they pretty much said to put a stop to it, or it could possibly get worse. So that’s the decision that we made.”

The 23-year-old said he couldn’t recall it occurring on one particular play, but the pain has affected him on both sides of the ball, particularly when swinging a bat. Through 70 games this season, he was hitting .220 with a .594 OPS.

“Some days it’s to the extent where I could barely close my glove on defense, and then other days it’s just I feel a little bit like when I swing,” he said. “Some days better than others, but definitely feel it when I swing.”

Mayer is the fourth Red Sox infielder to land on the IL over the last five weeks. He originally moved from second base to shortstop when Trevor Story went on the IL on May 16 with a sports hernia.

Infielder Nick Sogard, who had been called up in Story’s place, hit the IL with a right oblique strain June 3, and Isiah Kiner-Falefa went to the IL with a forearm bone stress reaction similar to Mayer’s on June 20. Interim manager Chad Tracy said Mayer and Kiner-Falefa had imaging done, and Kiner-Falefa’s stress reaction is worse than Mayer’s, but both have been prescribed a period of rest before they’ll be reassessed.

Mayer hoped he could return sooner rather than later, particularly with Story on the IL. Story has been ramping up his own progression and began taking groundballs in the infield this week. He’s eligible to return shortly after the All-Star break and remains hopeful he can hit that mark.

Nevertheless, the revolving door of infielders has made an already tough season for the Red Sox even more challenging.

“We’ve taken some hits,” Tracy said. “Not just on infield, but on the pitching side with Garrett (Crochet). It’s part of the season, you just have to move on, next guy up to help us, and go out and win a ballgame. But yeah, we’ve certainly taken more hits on the infield side than anything else.”

Mayer has dealt with a series of injuries since being drafted in the first round in 2021. Last season, his first in the majors, he landed on the IL in August with a wrist injury that required surgery. In the minors, Mayer missed time for shoulder and back injuries.

“I want to be out there playing more than anybody,” Mayer said. “If it was up to me, I would still be playing. Like I said, I’ve been dealing with this for two months, so it’s nothing really new. We just came to the conclusion that if I kept playing, it could get worse.”

In Mayer’s absence, the Red Sox recalled infielder Tsung-Che Cheng, whom they claimed off waivers in February. Cheng was hitting .254 at Triple-A Worcester, with 37 starts at short and 23 at second.

Tracy said Cheng would get a majority of the playing time at shortstop in the immediate future, but Cheng will mix around the infield with Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler, who was called up when Kiner-Falefa went down last week.

Meanwhile, infielder Romy Gonzalez, rehabbing from shoulder surgery he had in March, is still rehabbing in Worcester but could return as soon as this weekend to help the beleaguered infield.

“It’s not ideal; none of us wanted this to happen,” Mayer said of so many infielders out. “None of us want to be hurt. We all want to be out there. We want to be playing, we want to be playing well for everybody, for the fans, for the city, for each other. So it’s definitely not the most ideal situation, but it’s where we’re at. We’ve just got to keep grinding and keep trying to get better.”
